chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fadala from Aban from Zurara who said:
I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about the time for the fasting person to break their fast, and he said, 'When three stars appear.'
And he said to a man who thought the sun had set and thus broke his fast, then saw the sun afterwards, he said, 'There is no making up (qada) required of him.'

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: What this report contains regarding the appearance of three stars is not what is relied upon, and what is observed is what we previously mentioned regarding the falling of the disc, and its sign is the disappearance of the redness from the eastern side, and this was what the companions of Abu al-Khattab (may God curse them) relied upon.

key_terms.سُقُوطِ الْقُرْصِ: Falling of the disc (of the sun)

ai.seo_question: What is the correct sign for breaking the fast according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith illustrates the evolution of fiqh regarding iftar by contrasting the literal interpretation of Imam al-Sadiq’s report (appearance of three stars) with the established juristic consensus (disappearance of redness after sunset). Muhammad ibn al-Hasan explicitly critiques the followers of Abu al-Khattab for relying on the star sighting, thereby anchoring the practical ruling in the more precise astronomical marker of the sun's disc disappearance and the subsequent fading of twilight redness. This distinction highlights the Shia scholarly method of reconciling narrations with observable natural signs to determine the exact moment for breaking the fast.
